tagline: A billion voices, a thousand traditions
overview:
India is home to more people than any other country, about 1.4 billion, roughly one in every six humans on Earth. It fills most of the South Asian subcontinent, a giant triangle of land that juts into the Indian Ocean, bordered by Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. At about 3.3 million km² it is the seventh-largest country, about one-third the size of the United States.

The capital, New Delhi, sits in the north; Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru are other giant cities. Hindi and English are used nationwide, and the constitution recognizes 22 languages, including Tamil, Bengali, Telugu and Marathi, each with tens of millions of speakers and often its own alphabet. Four major religions, Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, were born here, and India also has one of the world's largest Muslim populations.

India is the world's largest democracy, a federal republic of 28 states with an elected parliament and prime minister. It is a land of farmers and software engineers, ancient temples and space rockets, spicy street food and the world's biggest film industry.
landAndNature:
The Himalayas wall off northern India with the highest mountains on Earth, including Kangchenjunga, about 8,590 meters. Below them stretch the hot, crowded plains of the Ganges, a river sacred to Hindus. The Thar Desert bakes in the northwest, the Deccan Plateau fills the south, and rainforest drapes the Western Ghats along the coast. Each summer the monsoon sweeps in from the sea, delivering most of the year's rain in a few months.

India has more wild tigers than any other country, more than 3,000, along with Asian elephants, one-horned rhinos in Kaziranga, the last Asiatic lions in the Gir Forest, snow leopards, king cobras and the peacock, the national bird. In the Sundarbans, tigers swim between mangrove islands.
peopleAndCulture:
Indian life is a festival of color. Diwali fills homes with oil lamps and fireworks, Holi turns streets into clouds of colored powder, and Eid, Christmas and Sikh Vaisakhi are celebrated too. Food varies by region: wheat breads and rich curries in the north, rice, dosas and coconut in the south, and chai tea everywhere. More people are vegetarian in India than anywhere else.

Cricket is followed with wild devotion, and kabaddi, hockey and chess are also popular; chess itself began in India as chaturanga. Bollywood in Mumbai makes more films than any other place, full of song and dance. Yoga, classical dances like Bharatanatyam, sitar music and the ancient Sanskrit epics the Ramayana and Mahabharata remain part of daily culture. Indian mathematicians gave the world the decimal system and the concept of zero.
history:
The Indus Valley Civilization built planned brick cities with drains and baths about 4,500 years ago. Later came the Vedic age, the Buddha's teachings, and great empires: the Maurya under Ashoka, who spread Buddhism, and the Gupta, a golden age of science and art. From the 1500s the Mughal emperors ruled much of India and built the Taj Mahal.

British traders arrived in the 1600s, and by 1858 Britain ruled India directly. Mahatma Gandhi led a nonviolent struggle for freedom, and India became independent on August 15, 1947. The country was partitioned into India and Pakistan, uprooting about 15 million people and killing hundreds of thousands in violence; the region of Kashmir has been disputed between the two countries ever since. India adopted its constitution in 1950. It has since become a nuclear power, a technology hub and, in 2023, the first nation to land a spacecraft near the Moon's south pole.
funFacts: The Kumbh Mela pilgrimage draws tens of millions of people to the Ganges, the largest peaceful gathering of humans on Earth.
Indian Railways carries more than 20 million passengers a day and is one of the world's largest employers.
The game snakes and ladders began in India as a moral lesson about virtue and vice.
The word "shampoo" comes from the Hindi word champo, meaning to massage.
The Taj Mahal took about 20,000 workers and 22 years to complete, finished around 1653.
A floating post office operates on a houseboat on Dal Lake in Kashmir.
